events.title: BECK v. UNITED STATES: Certiorari denied; Feres doctrine upheld despite criticism
events.summary: The Supreme Court denied certiorari in a case challenging the Feres doctrine, which bars tort claims by servicemembers and their families for injuries incident to military service under the Federal Tort Claims Act. The petitioner, the widow of Air Force Staff Sergeant Cameron Beck, sought recovery for her husband's wrongful death after he was struck by a civilian federal employee driving a Government vehicle while off-duty. Justice Sotomayor's concurrence acknowledged Feres as difficult to justify and criticized for depriving servicemembers of redress, but voted to deny based on stare decisis and Congress's repeated failure to overturn it legislatively. Justice Thomas dissented, arguing the case should have been granted because the death occurred off-base and off-duty, outside the scope of military service.
events.why_relevant: The denial preserves a 75-year-old judicial doctrine that shields the Government from tort liability for servicemembers' injuries, despite acknowledged unfairness and near-universal criticism; the dissent and concurrence highlight unresolved tension over the scope and justification of sovereign immunity in military contexts.
events.basis: Feres's atextual expansion of the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA), 28 U. S. C. §2671 et seq., has garnered near-universal criticism; has caused significant confusion; and has deprived servicemembers and their families of redress for serious harms they have suffered during service to this country.

events.title: CLARK v. SWEENEY: Fourth Circuit reversed for abandoning party-presentation principle
events.summary: The Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed the Fourth Circuit's decision ordering a new trial in a murder case. The Fourth Circuit had granted relief on a constitutional claim (combination of juror, judge, and attorney failures) that the defendant never asserted in his federal habeas petition. The defendant had raised only an ineffective-assistance-of-counsel claim. The Court held that the Fourth Circuit violated the principle of party presentation by inventing a new claim and depriving the State of the opportunity to respond. The case is remanded for the Fourth Circuit to address the ineffective-assistance claim under the proper AEDPA standard.
events.why_relevant: The decision reaffirms the adversarial principle that courts must decide only claims the parties present, not claims courts devise sua sponte, protecting the integrity of appellate review and party autonomy.
events.basis: The Fourth Circuit transgressed the party-presentation principle by granting relief on a claim that Sweeney never asserted and that the State never had the chance to address.

events.title: PITTS v. MISSISSIPPI: Sixth Amendment confrontation right reversed on mandatory child-witness screening
events.summary: The Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed the Mississippi Supreme Court's decision upholding a mandatory statute that allowed screening of child witnesses from defendants during testimony. The Court held that the Sixth Amendment's Confrontation Clause requires case-specific judicial findings of necessity before screening, not mere reliance on statutory authority. The trial court had failed to hear evidence or make particularized findings; it simply invoked the statute's mandatory terms. The case is remanded for harmless-error analysis.
events.why_relevant: The decision reinforces constitutional limits on state statutory authority when it conflicts with federal constitutional protections for criminal defendants' confrontation rights.
events.basis: Under Coy and Craig, a trial court may not deny a defendant his Sixth Amendment right to meet his accusers face to face simply because a state statute permits screening.

events.title: Electricity shutoffs surge nationwide amid rising utility prices
events.summary: Data from utilities in 11 states show that residential electricity disconnections have risen in at least 8 states since the prior year, with some areas experiencing dramatic increases. In New York City, residential shutoffs in August were five times higher than a year prior. Pennsylvania saw a 21% rise in power shutoffs with over 270,000 households losing electricity. Overall, Americans are paying 11% more for electricity than in January 2025, with utility prices rising roughly three times faster than overall inflation. A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll found that 60% of Americans say they are spending more on utilities and blame Trump for rising prices.
events.why_relevant: Widespread electricity shutoffs and soaring utility costs affect millions of Americans' access to essential services and signal economic hardship that may influence political outcomes.
events.federal_nexus: Energy Secretary Chris Wright oversees federal energy policy and regulation.
events.basis: Data from select utilities in 11 states show that disconnections have risen in at least 8 of them since last year. In some areas, such as NYC, the surge has been dramatic - with residential shutoffs in Aug up fivefold from a year ago.

events.summary: Within weeks of Trump's second term, Target announced it was ending or scaling back key diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) pillars, including winding down racial equity programs, dropping diversity hiring goals, and walking away from a multi-billion-dollar commitment to Black-owned business investment. events.title: Congress amends Section 2 of VRA in 1982 to block laws with discriminatory impact
events.summary: In 1982, Congress amended Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act to block election laws with discriminatory impacts as well as those that purposefully aimed to suppress minority voters. events.title: Federal judge orders Newbern, Alabama to hold first legitimate election since 1965
events.summary: A federal judge ruled in 2024 that Newbern, Alabama must hold its first legitimate election since 1965 after the town's white officials locked Black candidate Patrick Braxton out of town hall and held a secret election to reinstall themselves, despite Braxton being the automatic winner under Alabama law after filing nomination paperwork in 2020. Braxton sued under Section 2 of the VRA, which prohibits voting laws or procedures that result in denial or abridgement of voting rights on account of race or color. On August 26, 2025, Braxton won the subsequent election by a count of 66 to 26.
events.why_relevant: The case demonstrates Section 2 of the VRA continuing to remedy explicit racial exclusion from political office and validates the law's ongoing necessity to protect minority voting rights and political participation.
events.federal_nexus: Federal judge enforced Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act against a municipal government.
events.basis: Braxton won his lawsuit in 2024, with a federal judge ordering Newbern to hold its first legitimate election since 1965. And on August 26, 2025, Braxton won again by a count of 66 to 26.

events.title: Supreme Court affirms Section 2 of VRA in Milligan v. Allen; rejects challenge to majority-minority districts
events.summary: In 2023, the Supreme Court affirmed Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act in Milligan v. Allen, rejecting a challenge to the constitutionality of drawing majority-minority districts to remedy racial vote dilution. Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh joined the court's liberals to affirm Section 2. However, in his concurrence, Kavanaugh suggested openness to the "temporal argument" that Roberts made in Shelby County v. Holder (2013), which struck down the VRA's preclearance provisions—the argument that while racial discrimination justified remedial action in 1965, it no longer does in 2023.
events.why_relevant: While Milligan appeared to settle the constitutionality of Section 2, Kavanaugh's concurrence signaled openness to arguments that would ultimately undermine the law, foreshadowing the Court's decision to hear Callais on the question of Section 2's constitutionality.
events.basis: Civil rights advocates had thought they'd dodged a bullet in 2023, when the Supreme Court affirmed Section 2 of the VRA in Milligan v. Allen, the lawsuit that led to Figures' district being drawn.

events.title: Supreme Court clarifies in 1986 that voting systems can be struck down for unintentional minority vote dilution
events.summary: In 1986, the Supreme Court clarified that voting systems could be struck down if they diluted the power of minority voters, even if the dilution was unintentional. events.why_relevant: The 1986 decision established the legal foundation for effects-based challenges to voting systems, enabling decades of subsequent litigation that has expanded minority political representation and is now under threat in Callais v. Louisiana.
events.basis: The Supreme Court then clarified in 1986 that voting systems could be stuck down if they diluted the power of minority voters, even unintentionally.

events.title: Supreme Court hears oral arguments in Callais v. Louisiana on VRA Section 2 constitutionality
events.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court heard oral arguments in October 2025 in Callais v. Louisiana, a case challenging the constitutionality of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. The case centers on whether drawing majority-minority districts to remedy racial vote dilution violates the 14th Amendment's equal protection clause. The plaintiffs raised a "temporal argument" on appeal—never litigated at the district court level—contending that while such remedial maps may have been constitutional in 1965, they are no longer justified today. The Court ordered reargument specifically on Section 2's constitutionality, surprising civil rights advocates who believed the issue had been settled in Milligan v. Allen (2023).
events.why_relevant: A Supreme Court decision striking down or narrowing Section 2 of the VRA would eliminate the primary remaining federal tool to challenge racially discriminatory voting laws and maps, potentially enabling a wave of gerrymanders and voter suppression across the South and affecting minority political representation nationwide.
events.basis: As the U.S. Supreme Court contemplates whether the VRA has outlived its usefulness, having heard oral arguments in October questioning the constitutionality of the landmark law's most vital remaining provision

events.title: Supreme Court strikes down VRA preclearance provisions in Shelby County v. Holder
events.summary: In 2013, the Supreme Court struck down the VRA's preclearance provisions in Shelby County v. Holder, which had required states and localities with particularly racist histories to obtain federal approval before changing any election laws. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that while the history of segregation justified preclearance in 1965, that was no longer true in 2013. Academic studies show the racial turnout gap has increased in the wake of Shelby County, particularly in counties once policed by the VRA's preclearance.
events.why_relevant: Shelby County eliminated the VRA's most powerful tool for preventing discriminatory voting changes before they take effect, and the "temporal argument" used to justify that decision is now being invoked in Callais to challenge Section 2 itself.
events.basis: In Shelby County v. Holder, the court invalidated the VRA's provisions that required states and localities with particularly racist histories to get federal approval before they changed any election laws.

events.title: DEA proposes 2026 aggregate production quotas for Schedule I and II controlled substances and assessment of annual needs for List I chemicals.
events.summary: The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) published a notice proposing 2026 aggregate production quotas (APQ) for Schedule I and II controlled substances and an assessment of annual needs (AAN) for ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, and phenylpropanolamine. The proposal reflects estimated medical, scientific, research, and industrial needs of the United States, lawful export requirements, and reserve stock maintenance. DEA considered seven statutory factors including net disposal trends, inventory levels, procurement requests, diversion extent, and information from HHS, FDA, CDC, and state Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs. The notice invites public comment through December 15, 2025, and the Administrator will issue a final order after consideration of comments or a hearing if held.

events.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency published a Notice of Funding Availability (NOFA) for the State Infrastructure Financing Authority Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act (SWIFIA) program. EPA estimates approximately $550 million in credit assistance available to finance over $1 billion in water infrastructure investment. Eligible applicants are state infrastructure financing authorities. Letters of Interest (LOIs) submitted on or after December 29, 2025, will be evaluated using specified statutory selection criteria. Projects must have eligible costs of at least $20 million, and EPA will provide up to 49 percent of estimated eligible total project costs.

events.title: EPA announces WIFIA program funding availability for water infrastructure credit assistance
events.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency published a Notice of Funding Availability (NOFA) for the Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act (WIFIA) program, announcing approximately $6.5 billion in available credit assistance to finance up to $13 billion in water infrastructure projects. The agency solicits letters of interest from eligible public and private borrowers for drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater infrastructure projects meeting statutory and regulatory eligibility requirements. Letters of interest submitted on or after December 29, 2025, will be evaluated using specified selection criteria across three categories: Project Readiness, Borrower Creditworthiness, and Project Impact.
events.why_relevant: This funding announcement represents a significant federal investment mechanism affecting water infrastructure development, project financing, and economic priorities across states and communities.
events.basis: EPA estimates that it may lend approximately $6.5 billion to help finance $13 billion in water infrastructure investment.

events.title: EPA approves Montana's Regional Haze State Implementation Plan for second implementation period
events.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency finalized approval of Montana's Regional Haze State Implementation Plan revision submitted August 10, 2022, satisfying Clean Air Act section 169A requirements for the 2018–2028 implementation period. The plan addresses visibility impairment in 156 national parks and wilderness areas through reductions in fine particulate matter, sulfates, nitrates, and precursor pollutants. EPA also approved the visibility component of Montana's October 1, 2018 Infrastructure SIP for the 2015 ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standard. The rule becomes effective December 29, 2025.
events.why_relevant: EPA approval of state air quality implementation plans is a core federal regulatory function that establishes enforceable pollution-control obligations affecting industrial operations, energy production, and environmental protection across jurisdictions.
events.basis: The EPA is approving a regional haze state implementation plan (SIP) revision submitted by the State of Montana on August 10, 2022 (Montana's 2022 SIP submission), as satisfying applicable requirements under the Clean Air Act (CAA) and the EPA's Regional Haze Rule (RHR) for the program's second implementation period.

source_meta.headline: Air Plan Approval; Montana; Regional Haze Plan for the Second Implementation Period

events.title: EPA publishes forty-eighth update to Federal Agency Hazardous Waste Compliance Docket
events.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency published the forty-eighth update to the Federal Agency Hazardous Waste Compliance Docket, a registry maintained under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA). The update, current as of October 3, 2025, identifies federal facilities managing hazardous waste or with reportable releases of hazardous substances. This update adds two facilities (Pacific Northwest National Laboratory Sequim Campus and US DOC NOAA NW Fisheries Science Center), deletes zero facilities, and makes zero corrections. The Docket now contains 2,399 total federal facilities subject to preliminary assessment and potential inclusion on the National Priorities List.
events.why_relevant: The Docket is a foundational transparency and accountability mechanism requiring federal agencies to disclose hazardous waste activities and environmental contamination, enabling EPA oversight and public access to information about federal facility environmental compliance.
events.basis: This document identifies the Federal facilities not previously listed on the Docket and identifies Federal facilities reported to EPA since the last update on April 21, 2025. Thus, the revisions in this update include two additions, zero deletions, and zero corrections to the Docket since the previous update.

source_meta.headline: Forty-Eighth Update of the Federal Agency Hazardous Waste Compliance Docket

events.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency published a notice of availability for six Environmental Impact Statements (EIS) filed during the week of November 17–21, 2025, pursuant to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and Clean Air Act Section 309(a). events.title: EPA withdraws direct final rule on steam electric power plant effluent notification dates
events.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) withdrew a direct final rule published October 2, 2025, that would have extended initial notification date requirements for steam electric power generating facilities under effluent limitations guidelines (40 CFR Part 423). The withdrawal was triggered by adverse public comments received by the November 3, 2025 deadline. A companion proposed rule remains open for comment, and the EPA will issue a subsequent final action addressing all comments without reopening the comment period.
events.why_relevant: Withdrawal of environmental compliance rules affecting power generation facilities demonstrates regulatory uncertainty and the reversal of administrative action in response to stakeholder opposition, affecting the stability of environmental governance.
events.basis: Because the EPA received adverse comment, the Agency is withdrawing the direct final rule entitled, 'Effluent Limitations Guidelines and Standards for the Steam Electric Power Generating Point Source Category—Initial Notification Date Extension,' published on October 2, 2025.

events.title: FCC Media Bureau seeks comment on network-affiliate broadcast television relationships and public interest obligations
events.summary: The Federal Communications Commission Media Bureau issued a notice requesting public comment on market, regulatory, and contractual dynamics between national television programmers and their local broadcast affiliate stations. The inquiry examines whether barriers exist preventing local stations from meeting public interest obligations, including potential network overreach, affiliate control over programming, compliance with existing affiliation rules, and good faith negotiation practices. Comment period closes December 10, 2025; reply comments due December 24, 2025.
events.why_relevant: The inquiry addresses whether dominant national networks are exercising undue control over local broadcast affiliates in ways that undermine local editorial independence and public interest obligations, raising questions about market concentration and regulatory enforcement in a critical information medium.
